title: Code Formatter
description: Code Formatter helps people format source code, structured text, and the destination workflow and review the result before using it in another system.
intro: Code Formatter is for a concrete handoff: take source code, structured text, and the destination workflow from a real task, produce the form the next editor, API, document, or workflow expects, and keep enough context to verify what changed.
audience: Developers, QA engineers, code reviewers, and technical writers
input: A representative sample of source code, structured text, and the destination workflow copied from the API, file, codebase, log, document, or request involved in the task.
outcome: A code formatter result that preserves the intended meaning and is ready to test in its destination.
review: Check source code, structured text, and the destination workflow, malformed input, escaped values, and destination-specific rules before relying on the result.
bestFor: Small and medium source code, structured text, and the destination workflow samples used for debugging, documentation, migration preparation, review, and reproducible tests.
steps: Paste a representative source code, structured text, and the destination workflow from the task you are working on.
Run Code Formatter and compare the first meaningful change with the source.
Inspect source code, structured text, and the destination workflow plus any destination-specific constraints.
Copy or download the result, then validate it in the editor, runtime, API, form, or publishing system where it will be used.
useCases: Code Formatter for a real development or integration task rather than a synthetic keyword example.
Preparing Code Formatter input and output for a bug report, documentation page, test fixture, or technical handoff.
Using Code Formatter to compare the source and result before a migration, import, release, or review.
Code Formatter helps catch structural or meaning-changing mistakes before the output reaches another system.

tips: Keep the original Code Formatter input beside the result until the destination check passes.
Use realistic source code, structured text, and the destination workflow instead of a one-word sample when validating Code Formatter.
Do not assume the visual cleanup from Code Formatter proves that source code, structured text, and the destination workflow is valid.
Run the normal project, API, schema, browser, or editorial validation after using Code Formatter.

faq.question: Who uses Code Formatter?
faq.answer: Developers, QA engineers, code reviewers, and technical writers use Code Formatter when they need to format source code, structured text, and the destination workflow before continuing work in another editor, system, or document.

faq.question: What should I paste into Code Formatter?
faq.answer: Paste a focused but representative sample of source code, structured text, and the destination workflow into Code Formatter. Include the nesting, punctuation, characters, or edge cases that affect the real task.

faq.question: What does Code Formatter change?
faq.answer: Code Formatter changes the representation needed for this task. Compare the output with the source to confirm that values and intended meaning remain correct.

faq.question: What should I check after using Code Formatter?
faq.answer: After Code Formatter, review source code, structured text, and the destination workflow, escaped values, malformed input, and the rules enforced by the destination system.

faq.question: Can I use the Code Formatter output in production?
faq.answer: Use the Code Formatter result as reviewed working output, then run the destination system's normal validation, tests, schema checks, or editorial review before production use.

faq.question: Does Code Formatter store my input?
faq.answer: Code Formatter has no account or saved-history feature. Even so, remove passwords, private keys, session cookies, personal data, and production secrets before using any online tool.

keywords: format source code, structured text, and the destination workflow
commonMistakes: Running Code Formatter with a sample that does not represent the real input.
Using the Code Formatter result without comparing it with the original source.
Skipping validation in the editor, runtime, API, or document that receives the output.
